title: The Choice
passages:
She rode the winch down with one arm through the tether loop and her heels braced, because the drum was slow and her hands wanted something to do.

"Thirty," Wren said in her ear. "Trim's clean. Say your floor."

"Thirty-eight," Sol said. "Thirty-eight and I come up like a good girl."

"You've got ninety seconds before the surge turns in that ward, and then the water inside moves like a stairwell."

"Then talk faster."

At thirty-one she turned her left hand into the lamp. The grease pencil was above the knuckles where it had been all season — her floor, her trim, the depth of the case, in a hand she'd been told was neat. The beam crossed it and slid off. She turned the hand over twice, the way you do with a door you're certain you locked. Wet skin, the crease of a knuckle, and nothing written on any of it.

So she said the numbers out loud, because saying them is what keeps them. *Thirty-eight floor. Fifty-two case.*

Past thirty-eight the cold stopped being weather and turned into arithmetic. What went missing down here stayed missing; that was the whole rule and it had never once been negotiable, and she went down it anyway with her hand out for the next number.

"Forty-one," the voice said.

"Forty-one," she said, and reached for the name of the woman holding her line and found a hole the exact shape of a word. She patted at it three times, like a pocket. Then she quit, because pockets don't fill.

"Forty-three," the voice said.

At forty-three the tether ended. The last wrap had a clip on it and the clip hung open in the water, a thread of rust coming off the spring, and below that there was no line at all. She let it go and swam on hose and wire and her own two hands. When she reached for the word for the drum she got nothing, so she said "the thing that pulls" and left it there.

"You're eleven past your floor," the voice said.

"I can count," Sol said, and could not have said what she was counting with.

The ward came up out of the dark as a row of black rectangles, doors, doors, doors, and then one standing open. Second landing. The dogging lever — the bar that seals a hatch — had been snapped at the hinge and the frame bent back far enough to put a body through.

She put her lamp through the gap.

White enamel a meter off, big as a coffin lid, laid flat on the tile. A man sat against it with his back to her, yellow fins, hood shoved off his head, mask hanging on his chest by its strap. One hand flat on the enamel, palm down, the way you hold a hand on a stove to find out if it's warm. On his hip, clipped where a man keeps the thing he's breathing from, a stubby bottle with *S.S.* stenciled on the shoulder.

Comfortable. She had that word. She also knew comfortable was the last station before a man couldn't be lifted.

On the side of the case one green bead of light guttered, went out, came back, went out.

Sol reached again for the name of the woman on her line and got the hole. She set her hand on the hatch frame and pulled herself through.

She got a fistful of his harness and pulled. "Diver. Dey. Look at me."

He turned his head easy as a man on a porch. The mask hung on his chest, swinging, and he didn't reach for it. "I'm comfortable," he said. "I came down for something. It was a good reason."

"Which way is up?"

He considered it like she'd asked about the weather somewhere else. Then he pointed sideways, politely, at the wall.

Warm, agreeable, and no up in him; past that station a man weighed more than he did. She got the spare mask off her thigh loop, thumbed the purge, and put it over his face, and his hands came up and held it like a bowl somebody hands you at a funeral.

"Clip in. Your line's on the tile behind me. Clip in and I'll do the rest."

"All right," Dey said, and did not move.

She reached for the clip on his chest strap and her fingers were fat and stupid with cold, and that was when a voice came out of the dark past the case.

"Are you here for the box."

Not a question. An accusation with the serial filed off. Sol swung the lamp and found a kid, ten maybe, cranking a yellow toggle in her fist — the manual winch control, the one that works when the drum's power doesn't. Her arm shook like a wire in wind, and she kept cranking anyway, one-handed, because one hand can't hold four degrees and she'd been proving it for a year.

Strapped to her chest with a belt cut from a seat, a smaller shape. A boy. Masked. The window of his little mask had fogged white on the inside and stayed fogged, each breath laid over the last and none of them clearing.

"I'm here for the people," Sol said.

"That's what the last one said. We're taking the people, he said, then he went off with my air and he's not back." Nia's chin came up. "You're not having it. I wound it by hand twelve months. You don't get to swim in and take it because a boat wants to be rich."

"Nobody's rich. Kid—"

"Don't call me kid. You've got nothing on your hand." The girl's eyes went over Sol's bare knuckles, then past her shoulder to the open clip swinging on the end of the tether, and something in her face closed like a shop at the end of a bad day. "No line, no name, no writing. You're one more boat-man come to take the box and leave."

Sol held out her spare mask, the good one, toward the boy on the girl's chest. "How long has he got?"

The charge cell sat in its housing on the case lid, a wound spring the size of a dinner plate, its light guttering green, holding, guttering, in the last quarter-arc of a dial with twenty-two years of somebody's arm behind it. The little mask fogged and did not clear. A spent canister — the cartridge that eats what you breathe out was done eating, and what came off the boy's next breath was his own exhaust going back in.

Two minutes for the boy. Three for the girl's arm. The surge turning somewhere above like a stairwell deciding to move.

"Take it," Sol said, and pushed the mask at her.

The girl set her chin and didn't.

On the net a woman's voice was saying her floor, saying trim, and Sol reached for the name that went with it and got the hole again, and left it. She kept the lamp on the fogged window of the little mask, where the breath clouded and did not clear, and the box ticked itself warmer, and two kids were running out of air in the dark.

She turned her back on the case and faced the hatch, because it is easier to do sums at a door than at a man who can't find up.

"Boat," she said. "I'm going to say this out loud. Correct me where I'm wrong."

"Go ahead," the voice said.

"Drum. The thing that pulls. What have you got."

"Ninety-one meters of line still on the barrel. Load rating two hundred fifty kilos. The drum's cell is in the same quarter-arc as that box, so you get one clean pull at full power, and then it's a hand on a toggle." A beat. "You're eleven past your floor and you're asking me for tonnage."

"Tonnage's the only thing down here that doesn't lie."

She counted them with her hand on them, the way you count cargo. Dey, eighty kilos of diver and steel fins, sitting. Herself, seventy-two with a bottle. The girl, thirty if she was wet, and the boy on her chest twenty more. Two-oh-five.

"Two hundred five," she said. "Two-fifty drum. That's a lift. That's a lift with margin."

Then she put her palm flat on the enamel and leaned. The case didn't rock, didn't shift, didn't do anything but sit there being heavy the way a full freezer is heavy, welded shut and packed to the lid with whatever the Factor wanted.

"Say a hundred eighty for the box," she said. "Three eighty-five against a two-fifty drum. The drum won't argue about it. It'll take us all off the tile and stop in the water and hang there while the surge comes through the ward."

"Two hundred and ten," the voice said. "I ran it while you were talking. It stops at eleven meters."

"Then that's a fact and not a plan."

Gas next. She lifted the stubby bottle off Dey's hip and turned the gauge into the lamp. Sixty bar, the needle steady as a stone. Her own was at ninety. The girl had a hospital cylinder lashed under the case housing with a needle so far into the red it was practically a rumor, and two people breathing off it.

"Two masks and a bottle marked S.S.," Sol said. "One man's ride from fifty-two to the top at the rate we'll be going up, and I've got to be at the top with my hands free working the line. So the arithmetic on air says two. The arithmetic on the drum says three, no crate. Neither one says four."

The girl stopped cranking long enough to look at her. "You keep saying sums like the box is money."

"It's twelve thousand to my boat."

"It's my brother." Her chin came up, gray-lipped, furious. "It's his medicine. All of it, the whole rest of it. Cold keeps it good. That's what my hand's been doing for a year — it isn't gold, it's the only cold thing in the world holding his medicine still. Cell dies, it goes warm, and then he's got a week instead of an hour. You want to weigh that on your drum."

Sol had nothing for that, so she said the rest of it plain. "Then I'll say what's in front of me. One line. One powered pull. A welded crate I can't cut loose in the time we've got, and three bodies, and air for two. The box or the people. Those are the only two answers on the page."

"Say the right one," the girl said.

"There isn't a right one. Somebody set the sum up wrong before we got here." She heard the water change before she felt it — the first pull at her fins, mild, patient, the stairwell above deciding to move. "Ninety seconds."

From the tile, agreeable as a man asked to pass the salt: "I could stay," Dey said. "It's warm here. I came down for something good."

"You did," Sol said. "It's in your pocket and you can't read it."

Then the green bead on the side of the case went out and did not come back, and a line of water ran down the white enamel from under the lid, and the girl's arm stopped in the middle of a crank with the yellow toggle hanging in her fist.

The drone settled a meter off Sol's mask, props hushed to a mosquito whine in the water. Its floodlights painted the ward in flat white, catching the rust on the door frame, the girl's gray lips, the fogged window of the boy's mask, the green bead dead on the case lid. A camera iris dilated. The Factor's voice came through the net with no static, no breath, no urgency at all.

"Count: one. Seals intact. Awaiting ascent."

Sol stared at the lens. The word *drone* sat in her head like a stone in a boot — she knew what it was, she knew who sent it, she knew what it wanted — but the name of the company that owned it had gone the same place as the woman on her line.

"Boat," she said. "Drone's here. Factor wants a count."

"Copy," Wren said. "Sol, the Factor's asking what goes up. The crate or the people."

Sol's hand found the hatch frame again. "Who's this?"

A pause. The drone's lights didn't flicker. "It's Wren. Topside. Winch."

"Wren." She turned the name over. No face came with it. No berth, no shift, no voice she could hang a memory on. "Wren. Say who's got my winch."

"Me. I've got the drum. I've got your line on the monitor — what's left of it. You're at fifty-two meters, eleven past your floor, off tether since forty-three. The surge is hitting the ward now. You have two minutes before the water in there moves faster than you can swim."

Sol's thumb rubbed the rust on the frame. "Feed it to me. All of it. No splices."

"Sol—"

"No splices. You said you'd correct me. Correct me now."

The drone's camera held on her face. The Factor's voice said, "Count: one. Awaiting your declaration."

Wren breathed once, audible over the net. "Two children. A girl, Nia, maybe ten. A boy, Teo, masked, fogged window, spent canister — he's rebreathing. She's been hand-winding the cell for a year. The cell just died. The case is warming. Teo has minutes. Nia has maybe three more. Dey is at your feet, eighty kilos, mask on but fogged, slate dark, no up behind the glass, comfortable — that's the word you used, comfortable. You're seventy-two, past floor, memory going. The drum has ninety-one meters, two-fifty rating, one powered pull left. The crate is welded, roughly one-eighty. Total with crate: three-eighty. Drum stops at eleven meters. Without crate: two-oh-five. Drum lifts. Air: your bottle at ninety bar, Dey's pony at sixty marked S.S., Nia's hospital cylinder in the red. Two people's air to surface at controlled rate. You need your hands free for the line. That leaves air for one more. The Factor's contract: twelve thousand credits, crate delivered seals intact. Your crew's berths on the highland arcology cost eleven-five. Three crew berths. Storm season declares in nine hours. The Marrow's mooring drowns at declaration. That's the whole page. No edits. You asked for it live."

The drone's iris didn't move. The Factor didn't speak.

Sol looked at the girl, at the boy's fogged mask, at Dey sitting warm against the dead case, mask fogged, slate dark, no up behind the glass. She looked at her own hand on the rusted frame, bare knuckles, no writing, no name for the voice in her ear.

"Say it again," she said. "The berths. Say what they cost."

"Eleven-five. Twelve thousand buys three berths with five hundred left for food and dock fees. Without the crate, you have zero. The Marrow loses its mooring. Three crew, no berths, storm season."

"Three crew."

"Three. Plus the two kids if you bring them."

"Three," Sol said. "And the box."

"The box is twelve thousand. The box is three berths. The box is the Marrow not drowning."

"Right." She let the frame go. "Right. Boat. Drone. Factor. You hear that?"

"Count: one," the Factor said. "Awaiting ascent declaration."

"Then declare," Wren said, quiet now. "Captain. Declare."
